stem: It is known that oxygenation can be improved by increasing the functional residual capacity. An increase in which of the following ventilator settings will lead to an increase in functional residual capacity?
explanation: Positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) increases functional residual capacity by maintaining positive airway pressure at the end of expiration. FRC is the volume remaining in the lungs after a normal passive expiration and reflects the balance between inward elastic recoil of the lungs and outward recoil of the chest wall. PEEP prevents dependent alveoli and small airways from collapsing at end-expiration, recruits lung units and increases end-expiratory lung volume, which can improve V/Q matching and oxygenation. Increasing FiO2 changes the oxygen concentration but does not itself increase FRC; respiratory rate and peak inspiratory flow do not directly provide sustained end-expiratory distending pressure. RACP pearl: PEEP primarily improves oxygenation through recruitment and increased end-expiratory lung volume.
tags: PEEP,Functional residual capacity,Mechanical ventilation,Oxygenation,Respiratory,2020 Feb MS

stem: Which lung volume is defined as the volume of air inspired or expired during a normal quiet breath?
option8: Forced expiratory volume in one second
explanation: Tidal volume is the volume of gas inspired or expired with each normal quiet breath. In a healthy adult at rest it is roughly 500 mL, although it varies substantially with body size and metabolic demand. This differs from inspiratory reserve volume, which is the additional volume that can be inhaled after a normal inspiration; residual volume, which remains after maximal expiration; and vital capacity, which is the maximal volume exhaled after a maximal inspiration. RACP pearl: tidal volume describes a single ordinary breath, not a maximal respiratory manoeuvre.
tags: Lung volumes,Tidal volume,Respiratory physiology,EMQ,Respiratory,2020 Feb MS

stem: Which lung volume is defined as the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a maximal forced expiration?
option8: Forced expiratory volume in one second
explanation: Residual volume is the worked answer and is the amount of gas remaining in the lungs after a maximal forced expiration. It cannot be measured directly by simple spirometry because it is never exhaled; measurement requires methods such as gas dilution or body plethysmography. Be aware that the wording of this recall is awkward: the 'volume exhaled from maximal inspiration to maximal expiration' would be vital capacity, whereas the volume left in the lungs after that maximal expiration is residual volume. The keyed answer therefore implies the question intended to ask what remains following full expiration. RACP pearl: RV remains after maximal expiration; VC is the volume moved from maximal inspiration to maximal expiration.
tags: Lung volumes,Residual volume,Vital capacity,Respiratory physiology,EMQ,Respiratory,2020 Feb MS

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with 5 days of worsening dyspnoea. What is the radiological diagnosis?
explanation: Right middle lobe collapse is identified by a triangular or wedge-shaped opacity in the medial right lower zone together with loss of the right heart border. The right middle lobe lies directly adjacent to the right atrium, so when it collapses medially the air-soft-tissue interface at the right heart border disappears: this is the silhouette sign. Subtle volume loss may also be present. Right lower lobe collapse more often produces a retrocardiac or posterior basal opacity and does not characteristically erase the right heart border in the same way. In a middle-aged or older patient, lobar collapse should prompt a search for an obstructing lesion; CT chest and bronchoscopy are common next investigations when malignancy or endobronchial obstruction is a concern.
tags: Right middle lobe collapse,Chest X-ray,Silhouette sign,Atelectasis,Respiratory,2022 Feb CA

stem: A 70-year-old man with an extensive smoking history presents with dyspnoea and persistent cough. Chest X-ray shows complete opacification of the left hemithorax with tracheal and mediastinal deviation toward the left. What is the most likely radiological diagnosis?
explanation: Left lung collapse is suggested by complete or near-complete opacification of the left hemithorax with volume loss and mediastinal/tracheal shift toward the opaque side. The direction of mediastinal shift is a high-yield discriminator in a 'white-out' hemithorax: collapse pulls the mediastinum toward the opacity, whereas a large pleural effusion usually pushes it away. In a 70-year-old smoker with persistent cough, an obstructing bronchogenic carcinoma must be considered as an underlying cause of total lung collapse. CT chest and bronchoscopy are typically required to identify the level and cause of obstruction.

stem: A 74-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer presents with progressive dyspnoea. BP is 100/80 mmHg, HR 90/min and SpO2 97% on room air. Chest X-ray shows marked smooth enlargement of the cardiac silhouette with a globular 'water-bottle' appearance. What is the most likely cause of her dyspnoea?
explanation: Pericardial effusion is suggested by the markedly enlarged, smooth, globular cardiac silhouette - the classic 'water-bottle' appearance. This sign generally requires a large effusion that has accumulated gradually, allowing the pericardium to stretch, which fits a patient with malignancy. Chest X-ray cannot determine whether tamponade is present: tamponade is a haemodynamic diagnosis supported by clinical findings and echocardiography. The relatively narrow pulse pressure in the stem raises concern, but the patient is not markedly tachycardic or hypoxaemic. Echocardiography is the key next test to quantify the effusion and assess right-sided chamber collapse and respiratory variation. RACP pearl: globular water-bottle heart in malignancy = large pericardial effusion.
tags: Pericardial effusion,Water bottle sign,Chest X-ray,Malignancy,Respiratory,2022 Feb CA

stem: A 23 year old female presents with several weeks of painful red lower limb nodules, arthritis and is found to have bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on a routine chest X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Sarcoidosis is the diagnosis, specifically a classic Lofgren syndrome phenotype. Lofgren syndrome is an acute presentation of sarcoidosis characterised by bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum and acute arthritis or periarthritis, classically affecting the ankles. Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disease with non-caseating granulomas; pulmonary and intrathoracic lymph-node involvement are common, while skin, eyes, heart and nervous system may also be involved. Erythema nodosum itself is a non-specific inflammatory lesion and does not contain sarcoid granulomas. The Lofgren phenotype generally has a favourable prognosis and may be diagnosed clinically in a typical presentation without tissue biopsy. RACP pearl: young adult + ankle arthritis + erythema nodosum + bilateral hilar adenopathy = Lofgren syndrome.
tags: Sarcoidosis,Lofgren syndrome,Erythema nodosum,Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy,Respiratory,2022 Feb CA

stem: A patient is found to have pulmonary hypertension on echocardiography and chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) is suspected. Which investigation is the best next screening test for chronic thromboembolic disease?
explanation: A ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan is the preferred screening investigation when chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension is suspected. CTEPH produces persistent mismatched segmental perfusion defects, and a normal perfusion scan makes clinically significant CTEPH very unlikely. CTPA is important for anatomical assessment and surgical planning but can miss more distal or subtle chronic thromboembolic disease, so it is not the most sensitive screening test. Right-heart catheterisation is required to confirm pulmonary hypertension haemodynamics, but it does not by itself establish thromboembolic aetiology. D-dimer is not useful for diagnosing chronic organised thromboembolic disease. RACP pathway: suspected CTEPH -> V/Q scan -> dedicated vascular imaging and right-heart catheterisation in a specialist centre.
tags: CTEPH,VQ scan,Pulmonary hypertension,Chronic thromboembolism,Respiratory,2022 Feb CA

stem: A haemodynamically stable patient develops a complete left-sided iatrogenic pneumothorax immediately after left subclavian central venous catheter insertion. SpO2 is 97% and RR 20/min. What is the most appropriate definitive management?
explanation: The worked answer is chest-tube drainage because this is a large/complete iatrogenic pneumothorax following subclavian central venous catheter insertion. Although the patient is currently haemodynamically stable, the extent of lung collapse makes definitive pleural drainage appropriate in the source framework. Small, minimally symptomatic iatrogenic pneumothoraces may sometimes be observed or managed less invasively, but a complete pneumothorax has a much lower margin for deterioration and is not treated simply by removing the central line. Needle decompression is reserved for tension physiology rather than a stable patient, while oxygen alone does not provide definitive drainage of a large pneumothorax. RACP pearl: management depends on cause, size and physiological compromise; tension pneumothorax is an immediate decompression diagnosis, whereas a large stable iatrogenic pneumothorax generally requires pleural drainage.
tags: Iatrogenic pneumothorax,Chest drain,Central venous catheter,Pleural disease,Respiratory,2022 Feb CA

stem: Which tumour has the highest association with neurological paraneoplastic syndromes?
explanation: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) has the strongest association with neurological paraneoplastic syndromes among these options. SCLC is a neuroendocrine tumour and is particularly prone to immune-mediated paraneoplastic disease. High-yield neurological associations include Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, limbic encephalitis and sensory neuronopathy; anti-Hu antibodies are a classic SCLC-associated marker. SCLC also causes endocrine paraneoplastic syndromes such as SIADH and ectopic ACTH production. Thymoma is strongly associated with myasthenia gravis, but across the broader spectrum of neurological paraneoplastic syndromes SCLC is the classic malignancy.
tags: Small cell lung cancer,Paraneoplastic neurological syndrome,Anti-Hu,Lambert-Eaton,Respiratory,2022 Feb CA

stem: A 50 year old male is admitted to the ICU with severe influenza A requiring mechanical ventilation. He becomes oligoanuric. These are his bloods: Cr 356, K 6.3, Na 142, Bili 16, AST 2300, ALT 300, ALP 200, raised anion gap, lactate 2.2. Which complication of severe influenza is responsible for the patient's overall clinical picture and biochemistry?
explanation: Rhabdomyolysis best unifies the biochemical pattern. Severe influenza can cause viral myositis with skeletal-muscle breakdown, releasing myoglobin, potassium, phosphate and muscle enzymes. The very high AST with a disproportionately lower ALT is an important clue because AST is abundant in skeletal muscle whereas ALT is relatively more liver-specific. Myoglobin-associated tubular toxicity and obstruction can produce severe AKI and oligoanuria, while release of intracellular potassium explains the hyperkalaemia. Creatine kinase, urinalysis for haem with few/no red cells and serial electrolytes would help confirm the diagnosis. Ischaemic hepatitis can produce very high aminotransferases but would usually require a compatible shock/hypoperfusion context and does not as neatly explain the hyperkalaemia and muscle pattern. RACP pearl: marked AST >> ALT plus hyperkalaemic AKI in severe influenza should trigger a CK and consideration of rhabdomyolysis.
tags: Influenza,Rhabdomyolysis,Acute kidney injury,Hyperkalaemia,Viral myositis,Respiratory,2022 Feb CA

stem: Which of the following allergens has the greatest association with thunderstorm asthma?
explanation: Rye-grass pollen is the classic Australian allergen associated with epidemic thunderstorm asthma, particularly in south-eastern Australia during spring and early summer. Storm updrafts lift pollen grains into moisture-rich clouds, where osmotic rupture releases much smaller allergen-containing particles. These particles are sufficiently small to reach the lower airways; downdrafts then concentrate them near ground level, producing sudden widespread bronchospasm in sensitised individuals. Patients with allergic rhinitis due to grass pollen may be at risk even if they have not previously recognised asthma. RACP pearl: thunderstorm asthma in Australia = rye grass pollen, with respirable fragments generated by storm-related pollen rupture.

stem: Preoxygenation is routinely performed before endotracheal intubation to increase safe apnoea time. Why is preoxygenation less effective in patients with obesity?
explanation: Reduced functional residual capacity (FRC) is the main reason preoxygenation provides a shorter safe apnoea time in obesity. Preoxygenation replaces nitrogen in the lungs with oxygen, so the oxygenated FRC becomes the principal reservoir available during apnoea. Obesity reduces FRC because abdominal mass pushes the diaphragm cephalad and chest-wall loading reduces compliance; supine positioning and anaesthesia worsen this further. Closing capacity may approach or exceed FRC, promoting dependent small-airway closure and atelectasis. Obese patients also have increased oxygen consumption, which accelerates desaturation once apnoea begins. RACP pearl: preoxygenation reserve = FRC; obesity reduces FRC and increases oxygen demand, so desaturation is faster.
tags: Obesity,Preoxygenation,Functional residual capacity,Intubation,Safe apnoea time,Respiratory,2022 Feb CA

stem: A 71 year old man presents with dyspnoea and a persistent non productive cough. He denies a history of loss of weight. He is a long-term smoker of the last 30 years. On examination, he is found to have significant proximal weakness and severe hypokalaemia. Imaging reveals a central pulmonary nodule with associated hilar lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Small cell lung cancer is the best fit. SCLC is strongly associated with smoking, commonly presents as a central/hilar mass with bulky nodal disease, and has a marked tendency to produce paraneoplastic endocrine syndromes. Severe hypokalaemia with proximal muscle weakness suggests ectopic ACTH production causing severe hypercortisolism. At very high cortisol concentrations, cortisol activates mineralocorticoid receptors, producing renal potassium loss, hypertension and metabolic alkalosis; cortisol excess also causes proximal myopathy and hyperglycaemia. This is distinct from the hypercalcaemia classically associated with squamous cell carcinoma through PTHrP. RACP pearl: central lung cancer + profound hypokalaemia/proximal myopathy = SCLC with ectopic ACTH until proven otherwise.
tags: Small cell lung cancer,Ectopic ACTH,Cushing syndrome,Hypokalaemia,Paraneoplastic syndrome,Respiratory,2022 Feb CA

stem: Pre-oxygenation is used in procedural sedation to increase safe apnoea time. Safe apnoea time is reduced in obese patients due mostly to a decrease in which of the following lung parameters?
option2: Forced expiratory volume in one second
explanation: Functional residual capacity is the critical parameter. Preoxygenation denitrogenates the lungs so that the FRC becomes an oxygen reservoir during subsequent apnoea. Obesity reduces FRC through cephalad diaphragmatic displacement and reduced chest-wall compliance, with further reduction in the supine position and after induction of anaesthesia. Obese patients also consume oxygen more rapidly, so the combination of a smaller reservoir and greater metabolic demand shortens safe apnoea time. DLCO, FEV1 and FVC may be altered in some obese patients, but they do not explain the preoxygenation problem as directly as reduced FRC. RACP pearl: safe apnoea time is largely about the size of the oxygenated FRC.
tags: Preoxygenation,Obesity,Functional residual capacity,Safe apnoea time,Respiratory,2022 Oct MS

stem: A patient has advanced COPD with FEV1 <30% predicted. Which intervention has the clearest evidence for slowing the long-term decline in FEV1?
explanation: Smoking cessation is the key intervention. Continued tobacco exposure accelerates the decline in lung function, whereas stopping smoking meaningfully reduces the rate of FEV1 loss toward that seen with normal ageing. Other COPD therapies are extremely important for symptoms, exacerbation prevention, exercise capacity and survival in selected groups, but smoking cessation remains the classic intervention specifically associated with slowing the long-term decline in FEV1. Long-term oxygen improves survival in severe chronic resting hypoxaemia rather than being prescribed to preserve FEV1, and pulmonary rehabilitation improves function and quality of life. RACP pearl: the single most important disease-modifying intervention for the trajectory of airflow limitation in a smoker with COPD is smoking cessation.
tags: COPD,Smoking cessation,FEV1 decline,Disease modification,Respiratory,2022 Oct MS

stem: A woman with diffuse systemic sclerosis has developed clinically significant interstitial lung disease. Which steroid-sparing immunosuppressive therapy is generally preferred as first-line treatment?
explanation: Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) is the preferred first-line immunosuppressive therapy in systemic-sclerosis-associated interstitial lung disease when treatment is indicated. The worked notes reference the Scleroderma Lung Study II, in which MMF and cyclophosphamide produced similar lung-function benefit but MMF was better tolerated, making it preferable for longer-term treatment. SSc-ILD most commonly shows an NSIP pattern, although UIP and other fibrotic patterns occur. Nintedanib can slow FVC decline and is useful as an antifibrotic in selected progressive fibrotic disease, but it is not the classic replacement for first-line immunosuppression in this question. Cyclophosphamide is effective but substantially more toxic. A practical additional pearl is that high-dose glucocorticoids are used cautiously in systemic sclerosis because of the association with scleroderma renal crisis.

stem: Which immune cell is most important in the early inflammatory pathogenesis of sarcoidosis and drives macrophage activation and granuloma formation?
explanation: T lymphocytes, particularly activated CD4-positive T cells, are central to the early immunopathogenesis of sarcoidosis. An unidentified antigen is presented to T cells, promoting a predominantly Th1-type response with cytokines such as IL-2 and interferon-gamma. These signals recruit and activate macrophages, which differentiate into epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells and organise into the characteristic non-caseating granuloma. Thus macrophages are major structural cells within established granulomas, but the option that best represents the initiating/acute immune cell response is T lymphocytes. RACP pathway: antigen -> CD4 T-cell activation -> Th1 cytokines -> macrophage activation -> non-caseating granuloma.
tags: Sarcoidosis,T lymphocytes,CD4 T cells,Granuloma,Th1,Respiratory,2022 Oct MS

stem: What is the mechanism of action of omalizumab?
option1: Anti-IL-5 monoclonal antibody causing eosinophil depletion
option2: Anti-IL-4 receptor alpha monoclonal antibody inhibiting IL-4 and IL-13 signalling
option3: Anti-IgE monoclonal antibody preventing IgE binding to mast cells and basophils
explanation: Omalizumab is an anti-IgE monoclonal antibody. It binds circulating free IgE and prevents IgE from binding to the high-affinity Fc-epsilon-RI receptor on mast cells and basophils; over time it also reduces receptor expression. This reduces allergen-triggered mast-cell activation and downstream type 2 inflammation. The distractors correspond to other asthma therapies: mepolizumab/benralizumab target the IL-5 pathway, dupilumab blocks IL-4 receptor alpha and therefore IL-4/IL-13 signalling, montelukast is a leukotriene-receptor antagonist, and roflumilast is a PDE-4 inhibitor. RACP pearl: omalizumab = anti-IgE, used in selected severe allergic asthma with an appropriate sensitisation/IgE phenotype.

stem: A 50-year-old man develops adult-onset wheeze and episodic breathlessness. Symptoms have not improved as expected with salbutamol and inhaled corticosteroid therapy, and the diagnosis of asthma has not yet been objectively confirmed. What is the next investigation?
explanation: Spirometry is the next investigation because the first priority is to confirm that the patient actually has variable airflow obstruction consistent with asthma before escalating therapy. Adult-onset symptoms that do not respond as expected should trigger reconsideration of the diagnosis, inhaler technique, adherence and alternative causes. Spirometry with bronchodilator testing is the standard objective first-line test. FeNO and eosinophil count can phenotype type 2 inflammation and support the diagnosis but are not substitutes for demonstrating variable airflow limitation. Bronchoscopy and CTPA are reserved for specific alternative diagnoses or red flags. RACP pearl: difficult 'asthma' should be objectively confirmed before being labelled treatment-resistant.

stem: A 40-year-old woman with newly diagnosed small cell lung cancer develops a photosensitive rash involving the face, upper chest and hands, with periungual change and Raynaud phenomenon. She has no myalgia or muscle weakness, and CK is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
option5: Vasculitic rash secondary to microscopic polyangiitis
explanation: Amyopathic dermatomyositis is the intended diagnosis. The distribution described is compatible with characteristic dermatomyositis skin disease: a heliotrope-type facial eruption, V-sign/shawl-type photosensitive rash and Gottron-type hand lesions; Raynaud phenomenon can coexist. The absence of myalgia or objective weakness with a normal CK supports the amyopathic variant, in which the typical cutaneous manifestations occur without clinically apparent inflammatory myopathy. Dermatomyositis has an important malignancy association, making the new small cell lung cancer highly relevant. Anti-TIF1-gamma is particularly associated with malignancy-associated dermatomyositis, while anti-NXP2 can also be linked. RACP pearl: classic dermatomyositis rash + normal CK/no weakness = amyopathic dermatomyositis; always consider associated malignancy.

stem: Which cancer is most commonly associated with neurological paraneoplastic syndromes?
explanation: Small cell lung cancer is the classic malignancy associated with the broadest range of neurological paraneoplastic syndromes. Its strong neuroendocrine and immunogenic phenotype is associated with antibodies such as anti-Hu and with syndromes including Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, limbic encephalitis, sensory neuronopathy and paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration. Thymoma has a particularly strong relationship with myasthenia gravis, but SCLC is the best overall answer when the question asks generally about neurological paraneoplastic syndromes.
tags: Small cell lung cancer,Paraneoplastic syndrome,Anti-Hu,Neurology,Respiratory,2022 Oct CA

stem: Thunderstorm asthma is mainly triggered in people with an allergy to which allergen?
explanation: Rye-grass pollen is the classic trigger for epidemic thunderstorm asthma in south-eastern Australia. During a thunderstorm, pollen grains can be lifted into humid air and rupture into microscopic allergen-rich fragments. These fragments are much smaller than intact pollen grains and can penetrate into the lower airways, while storm outflows concentrate them at ground level. Sensitised patients can therefore develop sudden severe bronchospasm over a very short period. Grass-pollen allergic rhinitis is an important risk marker, even in some people without previously diagnosed asthma. RACP association: Australian thunderstorm asthma = rye-grass pollen.
tags: Thunderstorm asthma,Rye grass pollen,Aeroallergen,Respiratory,2022 Oct CA

stem: Which of the following diseases is classically associated with predominantly upper-lobe pulmonary fibrosis?
explanation: Ankylosing spondylitis can cause a characteristic upper-lobe/apical fibrotic lung disease, usually after longstanding axial disease. It is uncommon but is a classic examination association. The distractors usually have different patterns: asbestosis predominantly affects the lower lobes and subpleural regions and is associated with pleural plaques; idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis classically has basal and peripheral UIP; rheumatoid-arthritis ILD is often UIP with lower-zone predominance; and systemic-sclerosis ILD is commonly an NSIP pattern with basal involvement. RACP pearl: upper-lobe fibrosis associations include ankylosing spondylitis, sarcoidosis and silicosis, while IPF/asbestosis are classically lower-zone diseases.
tags: Ankylosing spondylitis,Upper lobe fibrosis,Interstitial lung disease,Radiology,Respiratory,2022 Oct CA

stem: The emergence of a pandemic strain of influenza is best explained by which of the following mechanisms?
option1: Antigenic drift due to point mutation in haemagglutinin
option2: Antigenic shift due to reassortment of haemagglutinin and neuraminidase genes
option3: Direct spread of influenza B from avian reservoirs
option4: Gradual accumulation of mutations in nucleoprotein
option5: Recombination between rhinovirus and influenza A
explanation: Pandemic influenza arises through antigenic shift: a major antigenic change produced by reassortment of genome segments when two different influenza A viruses infect the same host cell. Influenza A has a segmented RNA genome and is classified by the surface proteins haemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N). Reassortment can generate a novel HA and/or NA combination to which the human population has little pre-existing immunity; if the new virus also transmits efficiently between humans, a pandemic can result. Antigenic drift is different: it is the gradual accumulation of point mutations in HA/NA and is responsible for seasonal variation and the need for repeated vaccine updates. RACP pearl: drift = small mutations/seasonal epidemics; shift = reassortment/new subtype/pandemic.

stem: A woman has an acute pulmonary embolism with right-heart strain on imaging but remains haemodynamically stable with limited symptoms. Which treatment provides the best overall clinical benefit?
explanation: Anticoagulation alone is the appropriate standard treatment for a haemodynamically stable acute PE with right-heart strain unless the patient deteriorates or develops another indication for reperfusion. Right-ventricular dysfunction identifies an intermediate-risk group and warrants close monitoring, but routine systemic thrombolysis reduces haemodynamic deterioration at the cost of substantially increased major bleeding and intracranial haemorrhage, without a clear overall mortality advantage in stable patients. Catheter-directed or surgical reperfusion is reserved for selected deteriorating or high-risk cases. IVC filters are generally used when anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated or in selected recurrent events despite adequate treatment. RACP pearl: RV strain without shock does not equal automatic thrombolysis.
tags: Pulmonary embolism,Intermediate-risk PE,Anticoagulation,Right heart strain,Respiratory,2022 Oct CA

stem: Which side effect of Ethambutol requires its discontinuation in the treatment of pulmonary tuberculosis?
explanation: Optic neuropathy is the characteristic dose-related toxicity of ethambutol and requires prompt cessation of the drug. Patients may develop reduced visual acuity, central scotoma and impaired red-green colour discrimination; toxicity can be bilateral and potentially irreversible if recognition is delayed. Baseline visual assessment and counselling about visual symptoms are therefore important, with more intensive monitoring in higher-risk patients such as those with renal impairment because ethambutol is renally cleared. Hepatotoxicity is much more characteristic of isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide. RACP pearl: ethambutol = optic neuritis/optic neuropathy and red-green colour disturbance.

stem: Smoking results in nonspecific elevation of which of the following tumour markers?
explanation: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) can be mildly and non-specifically elevated in smokers. CEA is most commonly used as a tumour marker in colorectal cancer follow-up rather than as a screening test, because numerous benign conditions and smoking can raise the concentration. This reduces specificity when interpreting a modest elevation. The key exam point is therefore that smoking is a recognised benign cause of raised CEA and a single elevated value should not be interpreted as diagnostic of malignancy.

stem: Each of these patients has a pleural effusion that is drained. They have normal serum albumin and glucose at the time of drainage. Pleural fluid: pH 7.1, LDH 1980, protein 54, glucose 2. What is the cause of the pleural effusion?
explanation: Empyema is the best match for this profoundly inflammatory pleural-fluid profile. A pleural pH of 7.1 is very low, LDH is markedly elevated, protein is high and glucose is low, reflecting intense neutrophilic inflammation and bacterial metabolism within the pleural space. In a parapneumonic effusion, a pH below about 7.20, low glucose, positive Gram stain/culture, frank pus or loculation identifies a complicated effusion that generally requires chest-tube drainage rather than antibiotics alone. An empyema is classically frank pus or a microbiologically infected pleural space. RACP pearl: pleural infection = low pH, low glucose and very high LDH; pH <7.20 is a drainage red flag.
tags: Pleural effusion,Empyema,Pleural fluid,Low pH,EMQ,Respiratory,2021 Feb MS

stem: Each of these patients has a pleural effusion that is drained. They have normal serum albumin and glucose at the time of drainage. Pleural fluid: pH 7.39, LDH 124 (50-100), protein 21, glucose 4.5. What is the cause of the pleural effusion?
explanation: Congestive heart failure is the worked answer and fits a relatively bland, transudative pleural-fluid pattern: near-normal pH and glucose with much lower protein and LDH than would be expected in infection or malignancy. Formal classification should use Light's criteria, which require paired serum protein and LDH values; the values in the recall are therefore suggestive rather than sufficient to calculate the criteria exactly. CHF commonly produces bilateral, often right-predominant transudative effusions from increased hydrostatic pressure. Diuresis can occasionally make a CHF effusion appear 'pseudo-exudative', in which case serum-pleural albumin/protein gradients can help. RACP pearl: CHF is the common transudate; pleural infection gives a much lower pH and glucose.
tags: Pleural effusion,Congestive heart failure,Transudate,Light criteria,EMQ,Respiratory,2021 Feb MS

stem: A 47-year-old non-smoker who works in an office presents with 3 months of dry cough and no systemic symptoms. Which diagnosis is most likely?
explanation: Extrinsic allergic alveolitis, now termed hypersensitivity pneumonitis, is the keyed answer. The source acknowledges that the recall is incomplete because the image was poor and no causative exposure is stated. HP is an immune-mediated lung disease caused by repeated inhalation of an antigen; acute/inflammatory disease can have centrilobular ground-glass nodules and mosaic attenuation, whereas chronic fibrotic HP often has upper-lobe or mid-zone fibrosis with air trapping. Sarcoidosis classically produces bilateral hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy, lung cancer is less likely in a younger non-smoker, and NSIP is a radiological/pathological pattern frequently associated with connective-tissue disease. In practice, a detailed exposure history and HRCT are essential before confidently diagnosing HP.
tags: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis,Extrinsic allergic alveolitis,Interstitial lung disease,Chest X-ray,Respiratory,2021 Feb CA

stem: A 65-year-old woman with metastatic adenocarcinoma of unknown primary presents with dyspnoea. BP is 100/85 mmHg, HR 127/min in sinus rhythm and SpO2 94% on room air. Chest X-ray shows a markedly enlarged globular cardiac silhouette. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Pericardial effusion is the keyed diagnosis. Malignancy is a common cause of large pericardial effusions, and the recalled CXR is described as resembling the classic enlarged globular or 'water-bottle' cardiac silhouette. More importantly, the physiology in the stem - tachycardia, low systolic pressure and very narrow pulse pressure - should make you assess urgently for tamponade rather than merely label an incidental effusion. Echocardiography is the decisive investigation, looking for a large effusion with right-atrial or right-ventricular diastolic collapse and exaggerated respiratory variation. RACP pearl: a water-bottle heart can suggest a large chronic effusion, but tamponade is determined by haemodynamics and echo, not CXR size.
tags: Pericardial effusion,Cardiac tamponade,Malignancy,Water bottle sign,Respiratory,2021 Feb CA

stem: A 60-year-old ex-smoker presents with 5 days of worsening dyspnoea and diffuse expiratory wheeze. Chest X-ray shows a medial right mid-to-lower-zone opacity with loss of the right heart border and evidence of volume loss. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Middle-lobe collapse is the keyed diagnosis. Right middle-lobe atelectasis classically produces loss of the right heart border on a frontal chest radiograph because the collapsed lobe lies against the right atrium; a wedge-like opacity may be seen in the medial right lower zone. In an older ex-smoker, lobar collapse should not simply be attributed to mucus plugging: an obstructing endobronchial lesion must be excluded. CT chest helps identify an obstructing mass and bronchoscopy may be required for direct visualisation and tissue diagnosis. RACP pearl: right-heart-border silhouette loss localises pathology to the right middle lobe.
tags: Right middle lobe collapse,Atelectasis,Chest X-ray,Silhouette sign,Respiratory,2021 Feb CA

stem: A 37 year old female has a diagnosis of acute pulmonary embolism. Her BP is 110/85, and TTE shows RV dilatation. Which of the following interventions will reduce mortality?
explanation: Anticoagulation is the clinically appropriate answer for this acute haemodynamically stable PE with right-ventricular dilatation. IMPORTANT SOURCE NOTE: the worked recall bolded 'pulmonary artery endarterectomy', but that is internally inconsistent with an acute PE; pulmonary endarterectomy is definitive surgery for selected chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH), not routine treatment of an acute intermediate-risk PE. RV dilatation identifies increased risk and warrants monitoring, but routine thrombolysis in a stable patient increases major bleeding without a clear overall mortality advantage. An IVC filter is reserved mainly for an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation or selected recurrence despite adequate treatment. This key has therefore been corrected in the study bank rather than preserving a likely recall error. RACP pearl: acute PE + RV strain but no shock = anticoagulation and close observation; CTEPH = consider pulmonary endarterectomy.
tags: Pulmonary embolism,Intermediate-risk PE,Anticoagulation,Source correction,Respiratory,2021 Feb CA

stem: Preoxygenation is given before intubation to reduce hypoxaemia during the period of apnoea. In patients with obesity, which physiological change most directly reduces the effectiveness of preoxygenation?
explanation: Functional residual capacity is reduced in obesity and is the key reason safe apnoea time is shortened. Preoxygenation replaces nitrogen in the FRC with oxygen, creating the main pulmonary oxygen reservoir available after ventilation stops. Abdominal mass displaces the diaphragm upward, chest-wall loading reduces compliance and supine positioning/anaesthesia reduce FRC further; dependent airway closure and atelectasis may then occur. At the same time, oxygen consumption is often increased. The result is a smaller oxygen store being consumed faster. RACP pearl: obesity causes rapid peri-intubation desaturation because FRC falls and oxygen demand rises.

stem: A patient with end-stage COPD continues to smoke. Which intervention is most effective at slowing further decline in FEV1?
explanation: Smoking cessation is the classic intervention that most effectively slows the accelerated decline in FEV1 associated with continued tobacco exposure. Bronchodilators and other inhaled therapies improve symptoms and reduce exacerbations, pulmonary rehabilitation improves exercise tolerance and quality of life, and long-term oxygen improves survival in appropriately selected patients with severe chronic hypoxaemia; however these are not primarily used to halt the long-term rate of FEV1 loss. RACP pearl: if the question specifically asks what changes the trajectory of FEV1 decline in COPD, think smoking cessation.

stem: A 40 year old female presents with acute onset of dyspnoea. Her initial observations are as follows: HR 95, BP 110/75mmHg, SpO2 96% and respiratory rate of 25. Her ECG and bedside POCUS demonstrate right heart strain. She was subsequently found to have a pulmonary embolism on a CT pulmonary angiogram. Which of the following interventions has the best mortality outcome for this patient?
explanation: Therapeutic anticoagulation is the standard treatment with the best established outcome in this haemodynamically stable PE. Right-heart strain moves the patient out of the lowest-risk group, but in the absence of shock or sustained hypotension she is not a high-risk/massive PE. Routine thrombolysis in intermediate-risk PE may reduce haemodynamic decompensation but carries substantial major-bleeding and intracranial-haemorrhage risk and has not shown a clear net mortality advantage for stable patients. Surgical or catheter-based reperfusion is reserved for high-risk PE or clinical deterioration in selected patients. An IVC filter is not a substitute for anticoagulation and is generally reserved for an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation or selected recurrence despite appropriate treatment.
tags: Pulmonary embolism,Anticoagulation,Right heart strain,Intermediate-risk PE,Respiratory,2023 Feb CA

stem: A 65 year old female presents with shortness of breath. She has an extensive, 60 pack year smoking history. On examination she has signs consistent with superior vena cava obstruction and Pemberton's sign is positive. A CT scan demonstrates a R) UL mass. She subsequently has a supraclavicular lymph node biopsy. Which histological sub-type would be an indication for urgent chemotherapy in this clinical setting?
explanation: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is the intended answer because it is highly chemosensitive and can shrink rapidly, making systemic chemotherapy particularly useful in SVC obstruction caused by SCLC. In a patient who is not immediately threatened by airway compromise, cerebral oedema or haemodynamic instability, obtaining tissue diagnosis before definitive oncological therapy is usually important because treatment depends strongly on histology. Severe SVC obstruction may require urgent endovascular stenting for rapid symptom relief regardless of tumour type. Non-small-cell tumours may be treated with radiotherapy and/or systemic therapy depending on stage and molecular findings. Pemberton's sign - facial plethora/venous congestion when the arms are raised - is a clue to thoracic inlet/SVC obstruction.
tags: Small cell lung cancer,SVC obstruction,Pemberton sign,Chemotherapy,Respiratory,2023 Feb CA

stem: In a bronchoalveolar lavage, what is the most predominant cell type?
explanation: Alveolar macrophages are the predominant cell type in normal bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, usually accounting for the large majority of recovered inflammatory cells. They act as resident phagocytes and form a major first line of defence within the alveolar space. The differential cell count becomes diagnostically useful when this normal pattern shifts: lymphocytosis can support hypersensitivity pneumonitis or sarcoidosis, eosinophilia suggests eosinophilic lung disease, and neutrophilia may accompany infection, acute lung injury or some fibrotic disorders. Exact reference percentages vary between laboratories and sampling techniques, so the durable exam principle is simply that normal BAL is macrophage-predominant.
tags: Bronchoalveolar lavage,Alveolar macrophages,BAL differential,Respiratory,2023 Feb CA

stem: A patient develops a postoperative chylothorax after thoracic surgery. A chest drain is inserted and parenteral nutrition has been commenced to reduce chyle flow, but the leak persists. Which additional medical therapy is most appropriate to improve the chance of avoiding repeat surgery?
explanation: Octreotide is the best medical option. Chyle is lymph enriched with absorbed intestinal fat that normally travels through the thoracic duct into the venous circulation; thoracic surgery can injure the duct and cause a chylothorax. Initial management aims to reduce chyle flow while the leak heals, using drainage plus a low-fat/medium-chain-triglyceride diet or temporary parenteral nutrition depending on output and severity. Somatostatin or its analogue octreotide can further reduce enteric lymph production, probably through reduced splanchnic flow and lymphatic secretion, and is widely used despite the absence of large randomised trials. Persistent high-output leaks, malnutrition or failure of conservative management may require thoracic-duct embolisation or surgical ligation.

stem: A 60 year old male has known idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. He has the following investigations: 6MWT with desaturation to 86% on exertion; DLCO 45% of predicted; FVC 50% on spirometry; right heart catheter demonstrating pulmonary arterial mean pressure of 18mmHg. Which value is the strongest indication to list for a lung transplant?
explanation: The 6-minute walk test is the strongest listing trigger among the values given because exertional desaturation to 86% crosses the <=88% threshold used in transplant-listing frameworks for fibrotic ILD. The source notes that FVC and DLCO are also important, but their listing criteria often depend on a documented decline over time rather than one isolated low value - for example a substantial fall in FVC or DLCO over approximately six months. A mean pulmonary artery pressure of 18 mmHg does not establish pulmonary hypertension and is not itself a listing trigger. RACP pearl: in IPF, transplant referral should occur early; listing becomes more urgent with objective progression, oxygen requirement, significant exercise desaturation or pulmonary hypertension.
tags: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis,Lung transplant,6-minute walk test,Exertional desaturation,Respiratory,2023 Feb CA

stem: What is the most common cause of a spontaneous pneumomediastinum?
explanation: Asthma is the comorbidity most strongly associated with spontaneous pneumomediastinum among these options. Marked rises in intra-alveolar pressure during coughing or bronchospasm can rupture peripheral alveoli; air then dissects along bronchovascular sheaths toward the mediastinum, the Macklin effect. Patients may present with acute chest pain, dyspnoea, subcutaneous emphysema or Hamman crunch. Vomiting is an important differential because oesophageal perforation can also cause mediastinal air, but that represents a secondary and potentially life-threatening cause rather than typical uncomplicated spontaneous pneumomediastinum. RACP pearl: young patient with asthma/chest pain/subcutaneous emphysema -> consider spontaneous pneumomediastinum, while severe vomiting requires active exclusion of Boerhaave syndrome.

stem: A 63-year-old woman with newly diagnosed lung cancer develops a heliotrope-type periorbital rash that later involves the neck, upper chest, back and hands, with periungual erythema and Raynaud phenomenon. She has no muscle weakness, myalgia or arthralgia, and CK is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The source option says 'Amyotrophic dermatomyositis', but the intended diagnosis is amyopathic dermatomyositis. The characteristic rash around the eyes and over the upper chest/back and hands is compatible with heliotrope rash, shawl/V-sign disease and Gottron-type lesions, while periungual inflammation and Raynaud phenomenon fit the inflammatory-myopathy/connective-tissue-disease spectrum. Normal CK and absence of muscle weakness or myalgia support the amyopathic variant, in which characteristic cutaneous dermatomyositis occurs without clinically apparent myositis. The new lung cancer is an important clue because dermatomyositis is associated with malignancy, particularly in older adults. RACP pearl: classic DM rash + normal CK/no weakness = amyopathic dermatomyositis; investigate for associated cancer.
tags: Amyopathic dermatomyositis,Lung cancer,Malignancy association,Normal CK,Respiratory,2023 Feb CA

stem: A patient with systemic sclerosis develops progressive interstitial lung disease with pulmonary fibrosis. Which autoantibody is most strongly associated with systemic-sclerosis-associated interstitial lung disease?
explanation: Anti-topoisomerase I, also called anti-Scl-70, is strongly associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis and with systemic-sclerosis-associated interstitial lung disease/pulmonary fibrosis. The useful antibody contrasts are anti-centromere, which is more strongly associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis and pulmonary arterial hypertension, and anti-RNA polymerase III, which is associated with diffuse skin disease and scleroderma renal crisis. Anti-U1 RNP points more toward mixed connective tissue disease. RACP pearl: Scl-70 = systemic-sclerosis ILD; centromere = limited disease/PAH; RNA polymerase III = renal crisis risk.
tags: Systemic sclerosis,Anti-Scl-70,Anti-topoisomerase I,Pulmonary fibrosis,Respiratory,2023 Oct CA

stem: A tracheostomised patient is being assessed for use of a Passy-Muir one-way speaking valve. Which precaution is essential before the valve is applied to avoid acute airway obstruction?
option1: Ensure the tracheostomy cuff is completely deflated
option2: Keep the tracheostomy cuff inflated to prevent aspiration
option3: Increase PEEP before applying the speaking valve
option4: Occlude the upper airway with a tracheostomy cap
explanation: The tracheostomy cuff must be completely deflated before a Passy-Muir speaking valve is applied. The valve opens during inspiration through the tracheostomy but closes during expiration, redirecting exhaled gas around the tube and upward through the larynx to permit phonation. If the cuff remains inflated, exhaled gas cannot escape around the tracheostomy tube, which can cause rapid air trapping, dangerously high airway pressures and potentially fatal obstruction. Upper-airway patency and secretion management also need assessment, but cuff deflation is the essential safety requirement. RACP pearl: one-way speaking valve + inflated cuff = obstructed expiration.
tags: Passy-Muir valve,Tracheostomy,Speaking valve,Cuff deflation,Respiratory,2023 Oct CA

stem: A patient admitted to ICU with community-acquired pneumonia subsequently develops severe oral and ocular mucositis with a Stevens-Johnson-spectrum eruption. Which respiratory pathogen is most classically associated with this presentation?
explanation: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the classic infectious trigger of Stevens-Johnson-spectrum mucositis in association with respiratory infection. A related presentation is Mycoplasma-induced rash and mucositis, historically called atypical SJS or Fuchs syndrome when prominent mucosal disease occurs with little or no skin involvement. The mechanism is immune mediated, involving cytotoxic T-cell responses rather than direct bacterial invasion of the skin. This contrasts with conventional SJS/TEN, where medications are the most common triggers. RACP pearl: pneumonia followed by severe mucositis/SJS-like disease, especially with sparse skin lesions, should raise Mycoplasma.
tags: Mycoplasma pneumoniae,Stevens-Johnson syndrome,Fuchs syndrome,Mucositis,Respiratory,2023 Oct CA

stem: An ICU patient develops multiple cavitating pulmonary lesions. Blood cultures grow Fusobacterium necrophorum. Which primary site of infection should be sought as the most likely source?
explanation: The oral/oropharyngeal cavity is the most likely primary site. Fusobacterium necrophorum is an anaerobic gram-negative bacillus that colonises the oropharynx and is the classic cause of Lemierre syndrome: pharyngitis or tonsillitis followed by septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein and metastatic septic emboli, often to the lungs where they can cavitate. Thus cavitating pulmonary lesions are usually secondary septic embolic disease rather than evidence that the lung was the original focus. RACP pearl: Fusobacterium necrophorum + cavitating lung lesions = look for an oropharyngeal infection and internal jugular thrombosis.
tags: Fusobacterium necrophorum,Lemierre syndrome,Cavitating lung lesions,Oral infection,Respiratory,2023 Oct CA

stem: A 56-year-old man with a heavy smoking history presents with progressive proximal muscle weakness. CT chest demonstrates a central mediastinal/hilar mass. Biochemistry also shows hypokalaemia, raising concern for a paraneoplastic endocrine syndrome. Which malignancy is most likely?
explanation: Small cell lung cancer is the most likely diagnosis. In a heavy smoker with a central or hilar mass and prominent proximal muscle weakness, a paraneoplastic syndrome should be considered. The added hypokalaemia supports ectopic ACTH production with severe hypercortisolism: cortisol excess causes proximal myopathy and, at high concentrations, activates mineralocorticoid receptors to produce renal potassium loss, hypertension and metabolic alkalosis. SCLC is also associated with other classic paraneoplastic syndromes including SIADH and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome. Thymoma is strongly linked to myasthenia gravis but is less consistent with the smoking-related central lung mass and ectopic ACTH phenotype. RACP pearl: smoker + central mass + proximal myopathy/hypokalaemia = think SCLC with ectopic ACTH.
tags: Small cell lung cancer,Proximal myopathy,Ectopic ACTH,Paraneoplastic syndrome,Respiratory,2023 Oct CA

stem: A young Chinese man from Wuhan presents with chest discomfort. A few years back in China, he was told that he had a fluid filled lesion in his chest however he was not treated for this. His CT is shown below. What is the most likely organism involved?
explanation: Echinococcus granulosus is the intended organism. Humans are accidental intermediate hosts of the dog tapeworm and acquire infection by ingesting eggs shed in canine faeces. Larvae cross the intestinal wall and form hydatid cysts, most commonly in the liver and lungs; thoracic cysts may remain asymptomatic for years and appear as well-defined fluid-filled lesions. Cysts can enlarge, calcify or rupture, with rupture risking allergic reactions and dissemination. Treatment depends on size and location and may include surgery or percutaneous techniques with antihelminthic therapy such as albendazole. RACP pearl: chronic fluid-filled pulmonary cyst in an endemic/exposure context = consider hydatid disease.
tags: Echinococcus granulosus,Hydatid disease,Pulmonary cyst,Parasitic infection,Respiratory,2024 Feb MS

stem: A man presents with progressive dyspnoea. CT chest shows upper-lobe-predominant parenchymal change with bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. There is no history of occupational exposure to silica, beryllium or asbestos. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Sarcoidosis is the best answer because the stem deliberately provides no occupational exposure, whereas silicosis, chronic beryllium disease and asbestosis all require a relevant exposure history. Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disease characterised by non-caseating granulomas and frequently affects intrathoracic lymph nodes and lung parenchyma. Bilateral hilar/mediastinal adenopathy is classic; more advanced pulmonary disease can produce upper-lobe/peribronchovascular fibrosis and architectural distortion. Berylliosis can closely mimic sarcoidosis histologically, which is why the absence or presence of an exposure history is crucial. RACP pearl: upper-lobe disease plus hilar/mediastinal nodes with no exposure clue = sarcoid; occupational fibrotic diseases should come with an exposure.
tags: Sarcoidosis,Mediastinal lymphadenopathy,Upper lobe fibrosis,Occupational differential,Respiratory,2024 Feb MS

stem: A 60-year-old woman with stage IV NSCLC has persistent dyspnoea 2 weeks after talc pleurodesis. CT shows two symptomatic loculated pleural fluid collections that are not draining freely. Which intervention is most likely to improve drainage of the loculations?
option4: Insert an indwelling pleural catheter without addressing the loculations
explanation: The source keys intrapleural fibrinolytic therapy because the recurrent malignant pleural fluid is loculated after pleurodesis. Fibrinous septations can prevent effective drainage and leave separate pockets of fluid; intrapleural fibrinolytic therapy may break down septations and improve drainage in selected symptomatic patients. IMPORTANT RECALL NUANCE: a later 2024 Oct CA recall of a very similar scenario keys an indwelling pleural catheter, illustrating that malignant pleural-effusion management depends on whether the main problem is recurrent free-flowing fluid, failed pleurodesis, trapped lung or loculation. In real practice this requires pleural-specialist assessment and ultrasound/CT definition of the collections. This row preserves the Feb MS worked answer rather than forcing the later recall onto it.
tags: Malignant pleural effusion,Loculation,Intrapleural fibrinolytic,Pleurodesis,Respiratory,2024 Feb MS

stem: A patient with COPD is already receiving LABA/LAMA therapy. Which clinical feature would most strongly support escalation to include an inhaled corticosteroid in the context of ongoing exacerbation burden?
option2: Multiple hospital admissions for COPD exacerbations
explanation: The Feb 2024 worked recall keys multiple hospital admissions, reflecting persistent exacerbation burden despite dual long-acting bronchodilation. The source itself notes an important nuance: blood eosinophil count is a strong predictor of the magnitude of benefit from inhaled corticosteroids in COPD, while frequent moderate/severe exacerbations are the clinical reason to consider escalation. In current COPD thinking, the decision is therefore made by combining exacerbation history with the eosinophil count and any asthma features, rather than by either factor in isolation. ICS is not primarily added for dyspnoea or impaired quality of life alone and carries harms including pneumonia and local candidiasis. A later 2024 Oct recall of the same concept keys high eosinophils; both rows are retained because they reflect the different recall wording.
tags: COPD,Inhaled corticosteroid,Exacerbations,Blood eosinophils,Triple therapy,Respiratory,2024 Feb MS

stem: During normal ageing, which of the following spirometric or lung-volume measurements typically decreases?
explanation: Forced vital capacity decreases with normal ageing. Age-related loss of elastic recoil and changes in chest-wall mechanics lead to earlier small-airway closure and more air trapping, so residual volume tends to increase. Total lung capacity is relatively preserved or changes much less because the rise in RV offsets the fall in vital capacity. FEV1 also falls with age, often faster than FVC, while ordinary tidal volume is not the defining change being tested. RACP pearl: ageing -> elastic recoil down, RV up, FVC/FEV1 down, with TLC relatively maintained.
tags: Ageing lung,FVC,Residual volume,Respiratory physiology,Respiratory,2024 Feb CA

stem: A patient with stable COPD has been on a LAMA/ICS inhaler for 10 years. He presents with several months of dysphonia. ENT review with laryngoscopy shows white, friable mucosa over the larynx. Biopsy with Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver stain shows filamentous fungal material. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Candida infection is the most likely cause. Inhaled corticosteroids deposit locally in the oropharynx and larynx and suppress mucosal immunity, predisposing to candidiasis that can present with dysphonia, white plaques or friable laryngeal mucosa. Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver highlights fungal organisms and supports the diagnosis. The management principles are to treat the fungal infection, review whether the ICS remains indicated, and reduce future local steroid deposition with correct inhaler technique, mouth rinsing and a spacer where appropriate. Persistent dysphonia in a smoker or high-risk patient still warrants direct visualisation because malignancy can coexist or mimic infection. RACP pearl: ICS + dysphonia/white laryngeal plaques = local candidiasis until proven otherwise.

stem: A patient with COPD presents with palpitations. What is the most likely rhythm?
option3: Sinus rhythm with frequent atrial ectopics
explanation: Multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT) is defined by an irregular atrial rhythm with at least three distinct P-wave morphologies, variable PR intervals and a ventricular rate above 100/min. It is classically associated with severe COPD, hypoxaemia, hypercapnia and acute pulmonary illness, and can be exacerbated by adrenergic bronchodilator therapy or electrolyte disturbance. Unlike atrial fibrillation, discrete P waves are visible; unlike atrial flutter, there is no organised flutter-wave pattern. The most important treatment is correction of the underlying respiratory and metabolic trigger. RACP pearl: COPD + irregular narrow tachycardia + >=3 P-wave morphologies = MAT.
tags: Multifocal atrial tachycardia,COPD,ECG,Three P-wave morphologies,Respiratory,2025 Feb CA

stem: A 40-year-old non-smoker who works in an office presents with 3 months of dry cough. Chest imaging shows an upper-lobe-predominant interstitial process without a focal mass or classic bilateral hilar adenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is the worked diagnosis. It is an immune-mediated interstitial lung disease caused by repeated inhalation of an environmental antigen and may present with dry cough and dyspnoea. Chronic or fibrotic HP can show upper-lobe or mid-zone predominance, mosaic attenuation and air trapping. Sarcoidosis would be more strongly suggested by bilateral hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy, while a focal lung malignancy is less consistent with an interstitial pattern in this younger non-smoker. The key real-world discriminator is a detailed exposure history, supported by HRCT and sometimes BAL lymphocytosis or antigen-specific IgG. RACP pearl: when an ILD question suggests HP, actively search the history for birds, mould, farming or occupational/environmental antigen exposure.
tags: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis,Dry cough,Interstitial lung disease,Respiratory,2025 Feb CA

stem: A man in his 20s presents with a lower-limb rash and cough. CT chest shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy without significant parenchymal disease. Quantiferon Gold is negative. Spirometry shows FEV1 and FVC in the 80-90% predicted range. On 6-minute walk test, he desaturates to <90%. He is diagnosed with sarcoidosis and weighs 75 kg. What is the most appropriate next management?
explanation: Prednisolone 20 mg daily is the worked answer. Many patients with pulmonary sarcoidosis, particularly those with Lofgren-type acute disease, improve spontaneously and do not require systemic therapy. The feature pushing this patient toward treatment is objective physiological impairment on exertion: despite near-normal resting spirometry, he desaturates below 90% on a 6-minute walk, indicating clinically important pulmonary gas-exchange impairment. Moderate-dose oral glucocorticoid therapy is appropriate to assess responsiveness; pulse methylprednisolone is excessive for this presentation. Methotrexate is generally used as a steroid-sparing agent when prolonged treatment is required, disease is more severe/progressive or glucocorticoid toxicity becomes problematic. RACP pearl: sarcoidosis treatment is driven by symptoms, organ threat and objective functional decline, not by the mere presence of hilar adenopathy.
tags: Sarcoidosis,Prednisolone,6-minute walk test,Exercise desaturation,Lofgren syndrome,Respiratory,2025 Feb CA

stem: CURB-65 is used to assess severity and mortality risk in community-acquired pneumonia. Aside from urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure and age, which variable is included?
explanation: Confusion is the missing CURB-65 component. The score is: Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate >=30/min, low Blood pressure (systolic <90 mmHg or diastolic <=60 mmHg), and age >=65 years. Each criterion scores one point. CURB-65 estimates pneumonia severity and short-term mortality and can help guide site-of-care decisions, but it should not override important clinical features such as oxygen requirement, rapid deterioration, significant comorbidity, frailty or social circumstances. RACP pearl: C-U-R-B-65 = Confusion, Urea, Respiratory rate, Blood pressure, age 65.

stem: A patient with chronic liver disease has dyspnoea that worsens on standing and improves when lying flat. Oxygen saturations fall when upright. This is attributed to hepatopulmonary syndrome. What is the underlying mechanism?
explanation: Hepatopulmonary syndrome is caused by intrapulmonary vascular dilatation in the setting of chronic liver disease or portal hypertension. Increased pulmonary vasodilator signalling, including nitric oxide pathways, produces abnormally dilated pulmonary capillaries and intrapulmonary shunting. Oxygen molecules cannot adequately equilibrate across the widened vascular channels and perfusion is disproportionately directed to poorly oxygenated vessels, producing V/Q mismatch and diffusion limitation. The abnormalities are often most marked in the lung bases; standing increases blood flow to these dependent regions, causing platypnoea and orthodeoxia. Agitated-saline contrast echocardiography can demonstrate the shunt, while supplemental oxygen treats hypoxaemia. Liver transplantation is the only established definitive treatment with survival benefit.

stem: A 65-year-old woman with a 60-pack-year smoking history presents with facial swelling, distended anterior chest veins and Pemberton's sign. ECOG performance status is 1. A supraclavicular lymph node biopsy confirms lung cancer. Which histology would make urgent upfront chemotherapy the preferred initial treatment?
explanation: Small cell lung cancer is highly chemosensitive and is therefore the histology most likely to respond rapidly to urgent systemic chemotherapy in SVC obstruction. Whenever possible, obtain tissue diagnosis before oncological treatment because the choice of therapy depends on histology. However, severe SVC syndrome with threatened airway, cerebral oedema or haemodynamic compromise may require urgent endovascular stenting for immediate mechanical relief. NSCLC treatment is more dependent on stage, molecular profile, radiotherapy and systemic regimens. RACP pearl: SCLC is the lung cancer in which rapid chemotherapy response can be clinically useful for SVC obstruction.
tags: Small cell lung cancer,SVC obstruction,Chemosensitivity,Pemberton sign,Respiratory,2025 Feb CA

stem: A young patient develops marked wrinkling of the palms shortly after water exposure. A photograph shows wet, wrinkled hands. What is the most common associated condition?
explanation: Aquagenic wrinkling of the palms is strongly associated with cystic fibrosis and can also occur in CFTR mutation carriers. The skin develops exaggerated whitish papules and wrinkling within minutes of water exposure. The precise mechanism is not fully settled but is thought to involve abnormal salt handling in eccrine sweat glands and altered water transport, fitting the underlying CFTR chloride-channel disorder. Other reported associations include hyperhidrosis and some medications, so the sign is not absolutely specific. RACP pearl: unusually rapid/excessive palmar wrinkling after water exposure is a dermatological clue to CFTR dysfunction and should prompt consideration of cystic fibrosis in the right clinical context.
tags: Cystic fibrosis,Aquagenic wrinkling,CFTR,Dermatological sign,Respiratory,2025 Feb CA

stem: A 20-year-old patient with cystic fibrosis has 6 weeks of increased green sputum production. CT chest shows bilateral upper-lobe cylindrical bronchiectasis. There is no haemoptysis. Pancreatic and bowel function are normal. Which organism is most likely responsible?
explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a classic chronic respiratory pathogen in cystic fibrosis and is strongly associated with bronchiectasis, recurrent exacerbations and progressive decline in lung function. Green sputum is compatible with Pseudomonas because of its pigments, although sputum colour is not diagnostic and cultures are essential. In CF, newly acquired Pseudomonas may prompt an eradication regimen, whereas chronic infection may require inhaled suppressive antibiotics and treatment of acute exacerbations according to previous microbiology and sensitivities. Aspergillus is important when the phenotype suggests ABPA - asthma-like symptoms, very high IgE, eosinophilia and characteristic mucus plugging/central bronchiectasis. RACP pearl: CF bronchiectasis + recurrent green sputum = think Pseudomonas first.
tags: Cystic fibrosis,Pseudomonas aeruginosa,Bronchiectasis,Green sputum,Respiratory,2025 Feb CA

stem: A 46-year-old woman presents with a new acute pulmonary embolism. HR 94, BP 110/64. TTE shows right ventricular dilatation. She is not shocked. Which treatment has been shown to provide the greatest mortality benefit?
explanation: Anticoagulation is the appropriate treatment because this is a haemodynamically stable PE with RV strain - an intermediate-risk pattern rather than high-risk PE with shock. Anticoagulation prevents thrombus extension and recurrent embolisation. Routine thrombolysis or thrombectomy is not indicated solely because the RV is dilated; reperfusion strategies are reserved for haemodynamic collapse or selected clinical deterioration because they carry important bleeding/procedural risk. An IVC filter is not a mortality-improving alternative to anticoagulation and is mainly used when therapeutic anticoagulation cannot be given. The recurrence of this scenario across several recall years is itself high yield: RV strain changes monitoring and risk stratification, but stable BP means anticoagulation remains the core therapy.
tags: Pulmonary embolism,Anticoagulation,Right ventricular strain,Intermediate-risk PE,Respiratory,2025 Feb CA

stem: A patient presents with community-acquired pneumonia. CURB-65 score is elevated due to confusion, high urea, tachypnoea, hypotension and age >65. What is the main use of CURB-65?
option2: To determine duration of antibiotic therapy
option3: To estimate severity and help guide site of care
option4: To decide whether atypical cover is required
explanation: CURB-65 is a severity and mortality-risk tool that helps guide the appropriate site of care for community-acquired pneumonia. Increasing scores support hospital admission and, at the higher end, prompt consideration of senior review and critical-care assessment. It does not identify the infecting organism, dictate a fixed antibiotic duration or determine whether atypical coverage is required. Clinical judgement remains essential: severe hypoxaemia, rapidly increasing oxygen requirement, sepsis, multilobar disease, major comorbidity or frailty can justify escalation even with a lower score. RACP pearl: CURB-65 is a risk-stratification aid, not an antibiotic-selection algorithm.
tags: CURB-65,Community-acquired pneumonia,Severity,Site of care,Respiratory,2025 Feb CA

stem: A cirrhotic patient has dyspnoea and hypoxaemia due to hepatopulmonary syndrome. Which investigation is most useful to demonstrate an intrapulmonary shunt?
explanation: Agitated-saline contrast transthoracic echocardiography is the most useful test to demonstrate the intrapulmonary vascular shunting of hepatopulmonary syndrome. Microbubbles injected into a peripheral vein normally opacify the right heart but are filtered out by normal pulmonary capillaries. With intrapulmonary vascular dilatation they appear in the left atrium after a delay of several cardiac cycles. By contrast, an intracardiac right-to-left shunt tends to produce much earlier bubble appearance. Spirometry does not demonstrate a shunt, CTPA is not the standard diagnostic shunt test for HPS, and bronchoscopy is not relevant. RACP pearl: delayed left-heart bubbles = intrapulmonary shunt; immediate bubbles = intracardiac shunt.
tags: Hepatopulmonary syndrome,Bubble echocardiography,Intrapulmonary shunt,Agitated saline,Respiratory,2025 Feb CA

stem: A patient with stable COPD has been on inhaled corticosteroid therapy for many years and now has recurrent local fungal complications. Which factor would most strongly support ongoing ICS use in COPD?
option4: Mild airflow obstruction with no exacerbations
explanation: Frequent exacerbations together with an elevated blood eosinophil count most strongly support ongoing ICS therapy in COPD. The main benefit of ICS in COPD is reduction of exacerbations, and the likelihood of benefit rises with a higher eosinophil count, particularly when exacerbations continue despite appropriate long-acting bronchodilation or when there are coexisting asthma features. ICS is not primarily a treatment for isolated dyspnoea or chronic cough, and long-term exposure increases risks including pneumonia, oral/laryngeal candidiasis, dysphonia and skin bruising. In a patient with recurrent fungal complications, the indication should therefore be actively reviewed rather than assuming lifelong continuation. RACP pearl: COPD ICS decisions are driven by exacerbation history + eosinophilic/asthma phenotype, balanced against infection risk.
tags: COPD,Inhaled corticosteroid,Blood eosinophils,Exacerbations,ICS adverse effects,Respiratory,2025 Feb CA

stem: A patient with metastatic non-small-cell lung adenocarcinoma undergoes molecular profiling for targetable driver alterations. Which of the following receptor tyrosine kinase pathways is a common actionable driver in this setting?
explanation: EGFR is the best answer among these receptor tyrosine kinase pathways. Activating EGFR mutations are an important actionable driver in metastatic non-small-cell lung adenocarcinoma and can determine treatment with EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Molecular profiling in metastatic NSCLC is broader than EGFR alone and should assess for other actionable alterations such as ALK, ROS1, BRAF, MET, RET, NTRK and KRAS, depending on the clinical setting and testing platform. RACP pearl: metastatic non-squamous NSCLC requires molecular profiling because a targetable driver can fundamentally change first-line systemic therapy.

stem: A man with progressive dyspnoea undergoes CT chest, which shows upper-lobe-predominant parenchymal disease with bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. He has no relevant occupational exposure history. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Sarcoidosis is the best answer. The key discriminator in the recall is that no occupational or environmental exposure is provided: silicosis requires silica exposure, chronic beryllium disease requires beryllium exposure and asbestosis requires asbestos exposure. Sarcoidosis is a multisystem non-caseating granulomatous disorder that commonly involves bilateral hilar/mediastinal lymph nodes and can progress to upper-lobe/peribronchovascular fibrotic lung disease. In a typical asymptomatic pulmonary presentation, treatment may not be required because spontaneous remission is common; therapy is reserved for significant symptoms, progressive physiological impairment or organ-threatening disease. RACP pearl: exposure history is often the easiest way to separate sarcoid from occupational granulomatous/fibrotic mimics.
tags: Sarcoidosis,Upper lobe disease,Mediastinal lymphadenopathy,Occupational differential,Respiratory,2024 Oct CA

stem: A 60-year-old woman with stage IV NSCLC has recurrent symptomatic malignant pleural effusion despite recent talc pleurodesis. She requires an ongoing strategy for symptom control and repeated drainage. What is the most appropriate next pleural intervention?
explanation: The Oct 2024 worked recall keys an indwelling pleural catheter after recurrent symptomatic malignant pleural effusion despite recent talc pleurodesis. An indwelling pleural catheter allows repeated outpatient drainage and is particularly useful when pleurodesis has failed, fluid recurs or the lung does not fully re-expand. IMPORTANT RECALL NUANCE: the Feb 2024 MS version of a very similar loculated-effusion scenario keys intrapleural fibrinolytic therapy. Both answers can arise in different pleural situations: fibrinolytics target symptomatic septated/loculated collections that cannot drain, while an indwelling catheter is a standard strategy for recurrent malignant effusion/failed pleurodesis. Real management should therefore be guided by pleural ultrasound/CT, drainability, lung expansion and specialist assessment rather than by the wording 'two loculations' alone.
tags: Malignant pleural effusion,Indwelling pleural catheter,Failed pleurodesis,Loculated effusion,Respiratory,2024 Oct CA

stem: A patient with COPD remains exacerbation-prone despite regular LABA monotherapy and has had multiple hospital admissions in the past year. What is the most appropriate next inhaled maintenance step?
option3: Add ICS without adding a LAMA
explanation: Add a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) to create dual long-acting bronchodilation. In a patient already on a LABA with persistent exacerbations/hospital admissions, escalation to LABA/LAMA improves bronchodilation and reduces exacerbation burden more effectively than simply swapping one long-acting bronchodilator for another. ICS is added selectively rather than automatically, with greatest benefit in patients who continue to exacerbate and have a higher blood eosinophil count or asthma features. Because ICS increases pneumonia and local fungal risk, optimising dual bronchodilation is an important step before indiscriminate triple therapy. RACP pearl: symptomatic/exacerbating COPD on one long-acting bronchodilator -> usually LABA/LAMA first; then use exacerbation history and eosinophils to decide on ICS.

stem: A patient with COPD is already receiving LABA/LAMA therapy but continues to exacerbate. Which factor most strongly predicts benefit from adding an inhaled corticosteroid?
option2: Multiple hospital admissions irrespective of phenotype
explanation: A high blood eosinophil count is the best answer in this version of the recall because eosinophils predict the magnitude of exacerbation reduction from adding inhaled corticosteroid to LABA/LAMA. In practice, the decision is not based on eosinophils alone: ICS is most useful when a patient continues to have moderate or severe exacerbations despite optimal bronchodilation, particularly when eosinophils are elevated or there is an asthma overlap. Higher eosinophils strengthen the expected benefit, whereas low eosinophils make benefit less likely and infection risk relatively more important. ICS increases pneumonia and local candidiasis risk. RACP pearl: COPD triple therapy = exacerbation-prone patient + eosinophilic/asthma phenotype, not simply persistent dyspnoea.
tags: COPD,Inhaled corticosteroid,Blood eosinophils,Triple therapy,Respiratory,2024 Oct CA

stem: A young adult has suspected exercise- and aspirin-associated asthma, but baseline spirometry is non-diagnostic (FEV1 78% predicted). Which investigation is most useful for ruling out asthma when clinical suspicion remains?
explanation: Bronchial provocation testing is the most useful option for ruling out asthma when baseline spirometry is non-diagnostic but clinical suspicion remains. A direct methacholine challenge or an appropriate indirect challenge assesses airway hyperresponsiveness; a negative well-performed test has a high negative predictive value and makes current asthma much less likely. Bronchodilator reversibility is helpful when positive, but asthma is variable and reversibility may be absent between symptomatic episodes. Total IgE does not diagnose or exclude asthma. Exercise challenge can be useful when exercise-induced bronchoconstriction is specifically suspected, but the broader bronchial-provocation category is the best answer in this recall. RACP pearl: uncertain asthma after non-diagnostic spirometry -> bronchial challenge is useful to exclude disease.
tags: Asthma,Bronchial provocation,Methacholine challenge,Negative predictive value,Respiratory,2025 Feb MS

stem: A patient with severe asthma is being considered for tezepelumab. Which inflammatory mediator is directly targeted by tezepelumab?
explanation: Tezepelumab is a monoclonal antibody directed against thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP), an epithelial-derived 'alarmin' cytokine released early in the airway inflammatory cascade. By blocking TSLP, tezepelumab acts upstream of several downstream type 2 pathways and can reduce exacerbations across a broader severe-asthma phenotype than therapies restricted to IgE or IL-5 biology. Omalizumab targets IgE, while mepolizumab/reslizumab and benralizumab target the IL-5 pathway. RACP pearl: tezepelumab = anti-TSLP, an upstream epithelial alarmin-targeting biologic for severe asthma.

stem: In patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus, in which age group would the average HbA1c be expected to be lowest?
explanation: Children aged 9 years and below are the intended answer in this recall. Glycaemic control typically becomes more difficult during adolescence because puberty is associated with increased growth hormone and sex-steroid secretion, which increases insulin resistance, while psychosocial factors, variable meals and reduced adherence can further worsen control. Younger children historically had tighter parental supervision of insulin administration and meals, although contemporary targets are individualised and modern CGM/pump therapy has changed age-related patterns. The exam learning point is the deterioration in insulin sensitivity and glycaemic control that commonly accompanies puberty rather than a rigid modern HbA1c target by age.

stem: What is the most common cell type of a functioning pituitary adenoma?
explanation: Lactotroph adenomas (prolactinomas) are the most common functioning pituitary adenomas. Prolactin secretion is normally under tonic inhibition by hypothalamic dopamine acting at D2 receptors. A prolactinoma therefore causes hyperprolactinaemia with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, producing amenorrhoea/galactorrhoea in women and reduced libido, erectile dysfunction or infertility in men.
